rss.summary: Gemini Decisions API Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. rss.title: llm 0.37.2
rss.summary: Release: llm 0.37.2 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w . LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 . rss.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
rss.summary: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , gpus , claude-mythos-fable , recursive-self-improvement

AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. rss.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
rss.summary: Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send.
rss.text_excerpt:
Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send. Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. rss.title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
rss.summary: NaiveAI could potentially top Artificial Analysis’s speed rankings. Our hands-on test suggests its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek.
rss.text_excerpt:
Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. rss.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
rss.summary: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. rss.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
rss.summary: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

rss.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
rss.summary: Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such. Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn. From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran: I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map. what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...] Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps. each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound. The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for. There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location? I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app. And since I had one spare device, I then said: add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far Giving Claude Code ears I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears . Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone. I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket. Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem. I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not. Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun. Tags: projects , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , coding-agents , claude-code , claude-mythos-fable

github.text_excerpt: # Reflect Plain-file notes for Mac and iPhone: daily notes, wiki links, local search, and optional AI over your own Markdown. [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/team-reflect/reflect-open)](https://github.com/team-reflect/reflect-open/releases/latest) [![CI](https://github.com/team-reflect/reflect-open/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/team-reflect/reflect-open/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) Reflect is an open-source note-taking app built around a folder of Markdown files. It opens to today's note, lets `[[wiki links]]` connect people, projects, and ideas, and keeps search and backlinks fast without turning your notes into an app-only database. The app does not require a Reflect account. Notes live in a folder you choose, and optional services such as AI providers, transcription, iCloud, GitHub, or another git remote are connected directly by the user. ## Features - **Daily notes:** the app opens to today's note, and capture defaults there. - **Wiki links and backlinks:** type `[[` to link notes; each note shows what links back to it. - **Local search:** `⌘K` searches notes, backlinks, and tags. Optional semantic search can be enabled locally. - **Ask your notes:** `⌘J` can query notes through user-provided OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or OpenRouter keys. Answers cite source notes. - **Private notes:** `private: true` excludes a note's content from AI and other external services. - **Audio memos:** record audio and transcribe it into the daily note with a configured transcription provider. - **Browser capture:** save links, selected text, screenshots, and page text from Chrome. - **Sync choices:** use iCloud Drive for file sync, or git/GitHub for versioned backup. - **CLI:** `reflect today`, `reflect search`, and `reflect show` are available for scripts and agents. See [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md). ## Install 1. **Install the Mac app.** Download the latest release for your Mac: - **Stable:** [Apple silicon (M-series)](https://github.com/team-reflect/reflect-open/releases/latest/download/Reflect_aarch64.dmg) · [Universal (Intel and Apple silicon)](https://github.com/team-reflect/reflect-open/releases/latest/download/Refle [TRUNCATED]

# GAI **An all-in-one AI workspace for Godot game development: build and verify code with a desktop agent, then connect audio, image, and video tools through visual workflows.** GAI brings together a coding agent, reusable skills, command-line tools, and a lightweight Godot framework in one repository. Ask the agent to inspect a project, edit files, run commands, and execute tests—or connect processing nodes visually to build repeatable asset pipelines. ## Desktop Coding Agent ![GAI desktop coding agent](agent/asset/image/screenshot/gai_1.png) Complete the full loop from request to verification in a native Godot desktop interface: - Stream responses, command output, and file changes in real time - Use built-in `read`, `write`, `edit`, `delete`, `list_dir`, `glob`, `grep`, `bash`, `web_search`, and `web_fetch` tools - Run a model loop that calls tools, feeds their results back to the model, and repeats until it stops asking for tools or you end the run - Run multiple independent sessions and switch between them while agents are working - Preserve conversation history and pin frequently used sessions - Create workspace checkpoints before changes, with support for reverting conversations and files - Connect to OpenAI-compatible APIs with configurable models, endpoints, and proxies ## Visual Workflow Editor ![GAI visual workflow editor](agent/asset/image/screenshot/workflow_1.png) The workflow editor exposes repository skills as connectable nodes. Select an input, connect processing steps, and run the entire pipeline at once: - Browse skill nodes grouped into Input, Audio, Image, Video, and other categories - Connect type-safe `audio`, `image`, `video`, `text`, and `folder` ports - Process entire folders with batch iteration and glob matching - Execute nodes in dependency order while monitoring progress and logs - Save workflows as `.workflow.json` files and reopen them later - Switch between English and Chinese interfaces The screenshot above shows this audio pipeline: ```text Input folder → Batch for each → Convert to WAV → Trim leading and trailing silence → Normalize loudness → Standardize sample rate → Export to OGG ``` ## Features | Module | Capabilities | | --- | --- | | Agent | Understand codebases, edit files, run commands and tests, and search the web | | Workflow | Compose skills as nodes with batch processing, persistence, and execution logs | | AI |

# ◎ Paper Radar **Jev reads every new paper on arXiv each morning. You read the few that matter.** Also runs on [Claude (Haiku)](#use-claude-instead-of-jev) — same daily page, self-reported probabilities, [first-look calibration](docs/claude-calibration.md). Plain-English interests · calibrated probabilities · about 6 cents a day for *all* of arXiv · fork and go, no server [Quick start](#quick-start-5-minutes-no-server) · [Try the demo](#try-it-in-10-seconds) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Benchmark](#measured-against-real-reviewers-decisions) · [繁體中文](README.zh-TW.md) A real run: 50 new arXiv papers judged by Jev in 5 seconds for $0.002. No key? paper-radar demo shows the same page offline.
--- arXiv now receives more than 30,000 papers a month ([32,040 in June 2026](https://blog.arxiv.org/2026/07/09/arxiv-now-hosts-over-3-million-articles/)), about 1,500 per weekday announcement. Nobody reads the listing any more. Keyword alerts miss papers that use different words, embedding recommenders quietly drop whatever does not look like your past reading, and running a chat LLM over the whole firehose every day is slow and costs real money. Most AI tools read a paper and write you a summary. **Paper Radar does not write anything.** It asks [Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev) — TypeSafe's System One model — one yes/no question per interest and gets a probability back: *introduces an agent benchmark, 0.97*. Your repo's code decides what that means. Judgement instead of prose is what makes the arithmetic work. There is nothing to parse and no invented labels, and one judgement costs a fraction of a generated sentence — cheap enough to read *all* 1,500 papers rather than a pre-filtered handful, which is where keyword alerts and embedding recommenders lose the paper you actually wanted. | | Keyword alerts | Embedding recommenders | LLM digest bots | **Paper Radar** | |-----------------------|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:| | Reads every new paper | ✅ | ✅ | usually only a pre-filtered top-k | ✅ | | Understands meaning | ❌ | partly | ✅ | ✅ | | Explains *why* a paper matched | keyword | ❌ | free text | per-interest probability | | Thresholds you can tune and check | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ `cal [TRUNCATED]

## Overview Abyss is an open-source observability platform for AI agents. It observes agent-to-provider network traffic through a local proxy, helping developers and teams understand conversations, tool activity, token usage, and network failures without modifying agent source code or adding instrumentation to agent applications. Built in Rust, Abyss provides: - Explicit HTTP/HTTPS proxying and transparent proxying through macOS Network Extension and Windows WFP adapters. - Policy-controlled TLS interception and content capture for supported agent protocols. - Normalized events for model API protocols, including OpenAI's Responses API and Chat Completions API, and Anthropic's Messages API. - Plugins and Rust, TypeScript, and Python SDKs for custom integrations and event delivery. ## Install Install the prebuilt CLI on Linux x86_64 (with systemd) or macOS ARM64: ```bash curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL \ https://github.com/lexmount/abyss-rs/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh ``` ## Quick Start With Node.js 22+ and npm 10+ installed, start the local environment and run an installed agent through Abyss: ```bash abyss deploy-local start abyss run -- codex ``` Open the Abyss dashboard to explore sessions, model activity, and token usage: ```bash abyss dashboard ``` See the [Abyss CLI guide](https://abyss.lexmount.com/docs/product/open-source-software/abyss-cli) for configuration, capture controls, and lifecycle commands. ## Supported Harnesses and Models | Harnesses | Desktop | CLI | Web | | --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | | ChatGPT | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | |
